tool.title: Rick Sollo
tool.excerpt: Geraldo Antônio de Carvalho (5 December 1966 – 21 September 2026), better known as Rick Sollo or simply Rick, was a Brazilian singer, songwriter and producer of sertanejo music. He formed the duo Rick & Renner with singer Renner Reis, and had his successful compositions recorded by several sertanejo music artists. By forming the duo, he stood out as one of the rare black performers in modern sertanejo music and one of the most important names in the history of the genre. Sollo was reported missing after a helicopter carrying five people crashed near Urubici, Brazil. He was confirmed dead on 22 September 2026. == Early life and career == Geraldo Antônio de Carvalho was born in the city of Monte do Carmo, Tocantins on 5 December 1966. The son of Aldenora Cirilo de Carvalho, he developed a love for music through the influence of his father, Vitor Antônio, who always sang and composed songs for the Folia de Reis (a traditional Brazilian Christmas celebration). At just 10 years old, he began his musical career, and his first duo was with his sister Dalva, known as Sereno & Serenata. However, the duo didn't last long because, being a woman and part of a traditional family, her father forbade her from singing at night. Rick sought other partnerships, and in one of them adopted his current pseudonym, and the duo began their activities as Rick & Ray (names inspired by two members of Menudo). The duo lasted until Rick partnered with Renner in 1986, and from then on they began singing in nightclubs. For five years they only played gigs at night until recording an independent CD in 1991, but that CD is currently out of print. Their first officially recognized CD was released in 1992 by the Chantecler label, but their big break came in 1998 with the release of the song "Ela é Demais" (She's Amazing). For 25 years, the duo Rick & Renner sold over 10 million CDs. Rick also distinguished himself in music as a composer, writing highly successful songs recorded by artists such as Chitãozinho & Xororó, Gian & Giovani, João Paulo & Daniel, Gino & Geno, among others. tool.title: 2026 Ebola epidemic
tool.excerpt: The 2026 Ebola epidemic is an outbreak of the Ebola virus disease (EVD) mainly in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and neighbouring countries, including Uganda. Initial cases were reported on 14 May 2026 in the Ituri Province. It is the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC and began five months after the end of the previous outbreak. Early infections are theorised to have occurred in January or February 2026 in the town of Mongbwalu. By early August, it had become the fastest growing Ebola outbreak on record, as well as the second largest.

tool.excerpt: Black Robin, Once Down to Five Birds, Wins NZ Bird of the Year Wednesday, September 23, 2026 Headlines & Global News Subscribe World U.S. Business Tech Science/Health Sports Entertainment Trending Science/Health Science Black Robin, Once Down to Five Birds, Wins NZ Bird of the Year Every karure alive today descends from a single breeding pair, and its victory crowns one of the world’s most celebrated conservation recoveries. By Alan Simmons Published: Sep 22 2026, 4:44 AM EDT Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket FILE: A Chatham Islands black robin, or karure, wearing an identification band on its leg, perches on a branch in New Zealand's Chatham Islands on July 27, 2015. The critically threatened species, reduced to five birds in 1980, was voted New Zealand's 2026 Bird of the Year with a record 105,000 people casting ballots. Peter de Lange/Wikimedia Commons CC0 1.0 While much of the world spent the weekend counting ballots in rather weightier contests, New Zealanders turned out in record numbers for an election of their own — and handed victory to a small, entirely black songbird that 46 years ago was five individuals away from vanishing from the Earth. The karure, or Chatham Islands black robin, was crowned New Zealand's 2026 Bird of the Year on Monday, finishing atop the field with 26,610 votes, according to Forest & Bird, the independent conservation organization that runs the annual competition. The robin beat out two celebrated former champions — the kākāpō, the world's heaviest flightless parrot, which had led early voting, and the kārearea, New Zealand's native falcon — into second and third place. The turnout was itself a story. More than 105,000 people cast ballots, the most in the competition's two-decade history and roughly one in every 50 New Zealanders — up from about 75,000 last year and a world away from the fewer than 900 votes recorded in the contest's first edition. "Participation has really soared," said Rebecca Hatch, a group manager at Forest & Bird, noting that around 88 percent of this year's ballots came from within New Zealand — a relevant statistic for a competition that has weathered its share of electoral scandal, including accusations of Russian interference in 2019, when hundreds of votes arrived from Russian IP addresses, and a 2023 landslide powered by America
